title: Instant Pot Japanese-Style Beef Curry with Potatoes & Carrots
dek: Tender sirloin, chunky potatoes and carrots meet a glossy, mild Japanese-style curry sauce, with the roux stirred in only after pressure to prevent scorching.
image_alt: Japanese-style brown beef curry with whole potato and carrot pieces beside white rice and red pickles
ingredients: 1 3/4 lb boneless top sirloin steak, trimmed and cut into 1-inch pieces
2 large yellow onions, cut into 1-inch wedges
1 lb Yukon Gold potatoes, cut into 1 1/2-inch chunks
4 oz Japanese mild curry roux blocks, chopped
4 cups hot cooked short-grain white rice
1/3 cup fukujinzuke or other Japanese red pickles, optional

instructions.name: Season and brown the beef
instructions.text: Pat the sirloin dry and season with 1 teaspoon salt and the pepper. Select Sauté on High on a 6-quart electric pressure cooker, add the oil and brown the beef in two uncrowded batches for about 2 minutes per side. Transfer each batch to a clean plate.

instructions.name: Soften and deglaze
instructions.text: Add the onions and cook for 4 minutes. Add garlic and ginger and stir for 30 seconds. Cancel Sauté, pour in 1 cup broth and scrape the base until completely smooth with no browned bits attached.

instructions.name: Build the thin pressure base
instructions.text: Return the beef and its juices. Add the remaining 2 cups broth, Worcestershire, soy sauce and grated apple, then add potatoes and carrots on top. Do not add curry roux or honey yet. Confirm the contents sit below your model's maximum-fill line.

instructions.name: Pressure-cook and release
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 5 minutes; allow about 15 minutes for the pot to reach pressure. Let pressure release naturally for 5 minutes, then vent the remainder in short controlled pulses with hands and face away from steam. Pause immediately if liquid sputters and open only after the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Verify doneness
instructions.text: Check several beef pieces with an instant-read thermometer; each must reach at least 145°F, followed by a 3-minute rest. Potatoes and carrots should pierce easily but hold their shape. If any vegetable is firm, simmer it during the sauce-thickening step rather than pressure-cooking the sirloin again.

instructions.name: Thicken safely after pressure
instructions.text: Transfer 1 cup hot broth to a bowl and whisk in the chopped curry roux until smooth. Select Sauté on Low, stir the mixture into the pot and simmer 4 to 6 minutes, stirring and scraping often, until glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon. Add the remaining 1/2 teaspoon salt and optional honey only after tasting.

instructions.name: Serve mild-first
instructions.text: Cancel Sauté and rest the curry for 5 minutes. Spoon it beside hot rice, matching the plated presentation, and add optional red pickles. Keep the family pot mild and pass shichimi at the table.

why_it_works: Three cups of thin broth touch a fully deglazed base, while the dense roux stays out until pressure is gone, greatly reducing burn-warning risk.
Quick-cooking top sirloin and large vegetable pieces share one short pressure cycle, keeping the beef tender and the potato and carrot chunks recognizable.
Apple, soy and Worcestershire round out the mild curry blocks with sweetness, savoriness and acidity without making the sauce hot.
swaps: Boneless pork loin can replace sirloin by weight; cut it into 1-inch cubes and verify every piece reaches 145°F followed by a 3-minute rest.

For a dairy-free curry, check the curry-roux package carefully or make a paste from 3 tablespoons neutral oil, 3 tablespoons flour and 2 tablespoons mild Japanese curry powder, then whisk it in after pressure.
Brown rice is not a direct in-pot swap; cook it separately according to its package because it needs a different liquid ratio and schedule.
storage: Cool curry and rice in separate shallow containers within 2 hours. Refrigerate for up to 4 days and reheat with a splash of broth, stirring, until the curry and beef reach 165°F. Freeze the curry without rice for up to 3 months; potatoes will soften slightly after thawing.
notes: Total time includes two quick browning batches, about 15 minutes to pressurize, the 5-minute programmed cycle, a 5-minute natural release, controlled venting and final thickening.
Written for a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Follow your exact model manual's minimum-liquid, maximum-fill and venting instructions; never force the lid.
Curry roux contains starch and often sugar. Adding it before pressure can make a dense layer on the hot base, so this formula dissolves it after the lid is open.
Cut potatoes and carrots to the specified size so they hold their shape through the short pressure cycle.
Japanese curry-roux brands vary in salt and heat; begin with a mild product, taste after thickening and offer spice individually.

faqs.q: Why is the curry roux added at the end?
faqs.a: Its starch and sugar thicken quickly and may scorch during pressure cooking. Dissolving it in hot broth after pressure releases gives a smooth sauce and keeps thin liquid against the cooker base.

faqs.q: Why use top sirloin instead of chuck?
faqs.a: Sirloin becomes tender in the same short cycle that cooks the large vegetable pieces. Chuck needs a much longer cycle that would make the potatoes and carrots collapse.

faqs.q: What if my curry is too thick?
faqs.a: Stir in hot broth 2 tablespoons at a time on Low Sauté. If it is thin, simmer uncovered for another minute or two, stirring constantly because roux-based sauce catches easily.

title: Instant Pot Rajma Masala with Warm Roti
dek: Canned kidney beans turn into a thick, gently spiced North Indian-style tomato gravy while warm roti and an optional cool cucumber yogurt make it a complete busy-night meal.
image_alt: Bowl of thick red kidney bean rajma masala garnished with cilantro beside folded roti
ingredients: 1/2 tsp garam masala, plus more to finish
1/4 tsp Kashmiri chile powder or cayenne, optional
4 cans (15 oz each) red kidney beans, drained and rinsed
1/2 English cucumber, grated and squeezed dry
1/4 tsp ground cumin, for the yogurt
Chopped fresh chile or chile crisp, optional for serving

instructions.name: Make the cucumber yogurt
instructions.text: Stir the yogurt, squeezed cucumber, 1/4 teaspoon ground cumin, 1/4 teaspoon salt and 2 tablespoons cilantro together. Refrigerate while the rajma cooks.

instructions.name: Build the aromatic base
instructions.text: Select Sauté on a 6-quart electric pressure cooker and heat the oil. Cook the onion for 6 minutes until softened. Add ginger and garlic for 30 seconds, then stir in cumin, coriander, paprika, garam masala, turmeric and optional chile powder for 20 seconds.

instructions.name: Deglaze completely
instructions.text: Cancel Sauté, pour in the vegetable broth and scrape the base until completely smooth. Add the rinsed kidney beans and remaining 1 teaspoon salt. Spoon the crushed tomatoes over the beans in an even top layer and do not stir, keeping thick tomato away from the hot base.

instructions.name: Check the fill line
instructions.text: Confirm the contents remain below the half-full line used for beans and other foods that can foam; reduce the batch if your model manual requires it. The 1 1/2 cups broth must remain underneath the beans and tomatoes.

instructions.name: Pressure cook and release
instructions.text: Lock the lid and cook on High Pressure for 4 minutes; allow about 12 minutes to reach pressure. Let pressure release naturally for 10 minutes, then vent the remainder in short controlled pulses. Pause if liquid sputters and open only after the float valve drops.

instructions.name: Thicken the rajma
instructions.text: Stir thoroughly, then mash about 1 cup beans against the side of the pot. Select Sauté on Low and simmer 5 to 7 minutes, stirring often, until the gravy is thick but spoonable and reaches 165°F. Cancel Sauté and stir in lemon juice, another pinch of garam masala and most of the remaining cilantro.

instructions.name: Warm the roti and serve
instructions.text: Warm roti one at a time in a dry skillet for 20 to 30 seconds per side or according to the package. Spoon rajma into bowls, garnish with the final cilantro and serve beside folded roti and cucumber yogurt. Keep the pot mild and offer chile at the table.

why_it_works: Thin broth sits on a completely scraped base while crushed tomato stays on top, helping prevent the common electric-cooker burn warning.
Canned beans make this a true busy-night recipe; pressure drives the onion-spice flavor into them while partial mashing supplies a slow-simmered texture.
Warm folded flatbread matches the photographed meal, while the optional cool cucumber yogurt balances the concentrated tomato-spice gravy.
swaps: Cooked-from-dry kidney beans can replace canned beans only if they are already completely tender; use 6 cups cooked beans and keep the same short flavoring cycle.
For vegan rajma, use unsweetened plant yogurt for the cucumber side and confirm the roti contains no dairy.
Basmati rice can replace roti; cook 1 1/2 cups rice separately so the tomato-bean pressure formula remains unchanged.
storage: Cool rajma and roti separately within 2 hours. Refrigerate rajma and cucumber yogurt for up to 4 days and roti for up to 3 days. Reheat rajma with a splash of broth, stirring, to 165°F; rewarm roti in a dry skillet. Freeze rajma for up to 3 months, but do not freeze the yogurt side.
notes: Total time includes the onion sauté, about 12 minutes to pressurize, the 4-minute cycle, a 10-minute natural release, final simmer and overlapping yogurt preparation.
Written for a 6-quart electric pressure cooker. Follow your model manual's minimum-liquid, half-full bean limit and venting procedure; never force the lid.
This recipe uses canned beans so it does not rely on pressure cooking to make raw kidney beans safe. Never use an electric cooker's slow-cook function for raw red kidney beans.
Kashmiri chile is generally milder than cayenne, but brands vary. Omit it from the family base and add heat individually if needed.
Squeeze the cucumber well so the yogurt stays creamy rather than watery.

faqs.q: Why use canned kidney beans in an Instant Pot?
faqs.a: They make the meal realistic for a busy night and avoid variability from old or hard beans. Pressure still quickly infuses them with the onion-tomato masala while the natural release protects against sputtering.

faqs.q: Can I stir the tomatoes in before cooking?
faqs.a: Do not. Thick tomato on the base can scorch before enough steam forms. Layer it over the beans, then stir only after pressure has fully released.

faqs.q: How do I make the rajma thicker?
faqs.a: Mash more beans and simmer on Low Sauté for one or two additional minutes, stirring constantly. It will also thicken slightly during the five-minute serving rest.

title: Malaysian-Style Char Kway Teow with Prawns, Chicken & Bean Sprouts
dek: Wide rice noodles pick up smoky wok flavor with juicy prawns, tender chicken, fish cake, eggs and crisp bean sprouts in a balanced savory-sweet sauce.
image_alt: Malaysian-style char kway teow with wide rice noodles, whole prawns, chicken, bean sprouts and chives on a banana-leaf-lined plate
ingredients: 1 lb fresh wide flat rice noodles, gently separated
1 lb large raw prawns or shrimp, peeled and deveined with tails optional
8 oz boneless skinless chicken thighs, thinly sliced
1 tbsp light soy sauce, for the chicken
4 oz fried fish cake, thinly sliced
3 cups mung bean sprouts, rinsed and dried
1 cup garlic chives or scallions, cut into 2-inch pieces
Sambal oelek or sliced fresh chile, optional for serving

instructions.name: Prepare the noodles and proteins
instructions.text: Separate fresh noodles gently with your fingers; if refrigerated and stiff, microwave them covered for 30 seconds. Toss chicken with 1 tablespoon soy sauce and cornstarch. Pat prawns very dry and keep both proteins chilled until the wok is hot.

instructions.name: Mix the sauce
instructions.text: Stir the 3 tablespoons light soy, dark soy, oyster sauce, sugar, white pepper and water together. Set every remaining ingredient beside the stove because the cooking moves quickly.

instructions.name: Cook the chicken safely
instructions.text: Heat a 14-inch wok or 12-inch cast-iron skillet over high heat until a drop of water evaporates instantly. Add 1 tablespoon oil and spread the chicken in one layer. Stir-fry 3 to 4 minutes until browned and 165°F in the thickest pieces; transfer to a clean plate.

instructions.name: Cook the prawns
instructions.text: Return the wok to high heat, add 1 tablespoon oil and stir-fry the prawns for 2 to 3 minutes until opaque and 145°F. Transfer them to the chicken plate so they do not overcook.

instructions.name: Char the noodles
instructions.text: Add the final tablespoon oil, then garlic and fish cake for 30 seconds. Add the noodles and leave undisturbed for 45 seconds before tossing. Pour the sauce around the hot sides of the wok and toss for 1 to 2 minutes until the noodles are evenly bronzed.

instructions.name: Scramble and combine
instructions.text: Push noodles to the perimeter, pour eggs into the center and scramble until softly set, about 45 seconds. Return chicken and prawns with any juices and toss for 30 seconds.

instructions.name: Finish with crunch
instructions.text: Add bean sprouts and chives and toss just 45 to 60 seconds so they remain crisp. Divide immediately among warm plates, making the prawns and vegetables visible, and serve with lime and sambal at the table.

why_it_works: Cooking chicken and prawns separately gives each enough contact with the hot metal and lets both hit safe temperatures without steaming the noodles.
Fresh rice noodles need only a brief high-heat toss; resting them against the wok before adding sauce builds caramelized edges rather than a soft, wet texture.
Bean sprouts and chives enter last, preserving the crispness and fresh contrast visible in a well-made plate of char kway teow.
swaps: Use 12 ounces extra-firm tofu instead of chicken: press, cube and sear until golden before cooking the prawns.
For a shellfish-free version, increase chicken to 1 pound and replace oyster sauce with mushroom stir-fry sauce.
Dried wide rice noodles may be used, but soak or boil only until pliable according to the package, rinse cool and drain very thoroughly before stir-frying.
storage: Cool leftovers in a shallow container within 2 hours and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Reheat one portion in a very hot skillet with 1 tablespoon water until the noodles loosen and both chicken and prawns reach 165°F. Freezing is not recommended because rice noodles and sprouts lose their texture.
notes: A broad pan and genuinely high heat matter more than owning a traditional wok. If your burner is modest, cook the noodles in two batches and divide the sauce evenly.
Do not crowd raw protein or return it to the plate that held it before cooking; use a clean plate to avoid cross-contamination.
Fresh noodles vary in salt and softness, so taste the mixed sauce and reduce light soy slightly if your noodles are already seasoned.
The family base is not hot. Sambal belongs at the table so each diner controls the heat.
Total time assumes ingredients are fully measured before the wok is heated; the active cook is about 15 minutes.

faqs.a: They were probably cold or tossed too aggressively. Warm stiff fresh noodles briefly, separate them by hand and use a lifting motion rather than chopping through them with the spatula.

faqs.q: Can I get wok hei on an electric stove?
faqs.a: You can still build good char. Preheat a cast-iron skillet thoroughly, dry every ingredient and work in batches so moisture does not drop the surface temperature.

faqs.q: Can I make the sauce ahead?
faqs.a: Yes. Mix it up to one week ahead and refrigerate in a jar. Shake or stir before measuring because the sugar settles.

title: Colombian-Style Ajiaco with Chicken, Three Potatoes & Corn
dek: Three kinds of potato naturally thicken this Bogotá-inspired chicken soup, while corn, guascas, avocado, capers and cream make every bowl a complete cool-weather meal.
image_alt: Clay bowl of Colombian-style ajiaco with creamy potato broth, corn, avocado, capers and chicken
ingredients: 10 cups low-sodium chicken broth or water
1 lb russet potatoes, peeled and thinly sliced
1 lb Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 1-inch chunks
4 ears corn, shucked and cut crosswise into thirds

instructions.name: Make the chicken broth
instructions.text: Combine chicken, broth, onion, scallions, garlic, 1 teaspoon salt and pepper in a large heavy pot. Bring just to a boil, skim any foam, then reduce to a gentle simmer. Partially cover and cook 25 to 30 minutes until every thigh reaches at least 165°F away from bone.

instructions.name: Shred the chicken
instructions.text: Move the chicken to a clean plate. Strain the broth into a bowl, discard the spent aromatics and return the broth to the pot. When chicken is cool enough to handle, discard bones and shred the meat into bite-size pieces; refrigerate if it will wait more than 30 minutes.

instructions.name: Build the potato body
instructions.text: Add sliced russets, guascas and bay leaves to the broth. Simmer uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally and pressing some russet slices against the pot so they dissolve and thicken the soup naturally.

instructions.name: Add chunky potatoes and corn
instructions.text: Add Yukon Golds, red potatoes and corn. Simmer 20 to 25 minutes until the potato chunks are tender but still distinct and the corn is hot throughout.

instructions.name: Return the chicken
instructions.text: Discard bay leaves, stir in shredded chicken and simmer 5 minutes until it reaches 165°F. Taste and add the remaining teaspoon salt only as needed; broth brands and capers vary in salinity.

instructions.name: Serve the Bogotá-style bowl
instructions.text: Ladle soup into warm bowls with a corn piece in each. Top or serve alongside cream, capers, avocado and cilantro so diners can build the composed presentation. Offer lime if desired.

why_it_works: Thin russet slices break down into the broth, creating a creamy body without flour while waxier Yukon and red potatoes remain as distinct pieces.
Poaching bone-in thighs first builds a richer base and makes it easy to verify safe 165°F doneness before shredding.
Guascas supplies the characteristic herbal note, while cool avocado, briny capers and cream let each diner balance the rich potato soup.
swaps: If guascas is unavailable, use 2 tablespoons dried guascas ordered online rather than substituting oregano; for an emergency, use 1 tablespoon dried parsley plus 1 teaspoon dried tarragon for a different but gentle herbal profile.
Boneless skinless thighs may replace bone-in thighs; begin checking at 18 minutes and still verify 165°F.
For a lighter bowl, replace heavy cream with plain whole-milk yogurt, but add it at the table so it does not split in the pot.
storage: Remove corn pieces and cool soup in shallow containers within 2 hours. Refrigerate soup for up to 4 days and reheat gently, stirring, until chicken and broth reach 165°F. Store avocado, cream and capers separately. Freeze the soup for up to 2 months; potatoes will become softer after thawing.
notes: Guascas is an herb sold dried in Latin American markets and online; it is central to ajiaco's flavor and worth seeking out.
Do not let the soup boil hard after potatoes are added or the chunky varieties may break apart before the corn is ready.
The photographed bowl includes avocado and capers directly in the soup, so both are treated as essential serving components rather than decorative extras.
Total time includes chicken cooling and shredding while the first potatoes simmer.
Do not rinse raw chicken. Keep the plate used for cooked chicken separate from any surface that held it raw.

faqs.q: Why use three kinds of potato?
faqs.a: They do different jobs. Russets dissolve and thicken, Yukon Golds stay creamy, and red potatoes hold their shape, producing the layered texture that defines the soup.
Yes. Make the soup one day ahead, chill promptly and reheat gently to 165°F. Add avocado, capers, cream and cilantro only when serving.
Yes. Replace the ears with 4 cups frozen corn kernels and add them for only the final 8 minutes, though the bowl will lack the traditional cob pieces shown in the photograph.

title: Filipino-Style Bibingkang Galapong with Salted Egg & Coconut
dek: Banana-leaf-lined coconut rice cakes bake up tender and lightly chewy, with salted egg, queso fresco and grated coconut for a festive Filipino-style breakfast or dessert.
image_alt: Individual golden Filipino bibingkang galapong rice cakes baked in folded banana leaves with coconut and cheese
ingredients: 2 large banana leaves, thawed if frozen, or parchment paper
Melted unsalted butter, for the pan and leaves
1/4 cup melted unsalted butter, cooled slightly
2 cooked salted duck eggs, peeled and cut into 16 wedges
4 oz pasteurized queso fresco or mild feta, crumbled

instructions.name: Soften and cut the leaves
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 375°F. Pass banana leaves briefly over a low gas flame with tongs or over a hot dry skillet until glossy and pliable; do not char them. Cut eight 7-inch squares. Butter the leaves and press one into each well of a jumbo muffin pan, trimming only enough to keep them clear of the oven walls. Use buttered parchment if banana leaf is unavailable.

instructions.name: Mix the dry ingredients
instructions.text: Whisk rice flour, glutinous rice flour, baking powder and salt in a medium bowl, breaking up every lump.

instructions.name: Mix the batter
instructions.text: Whisk eggs and 3/4 cup sugar until smooth. Whisk in coconut milk, whole milk, melted butter and vanilla. Add the dry mixture in three additions, whisking only until no dry pockets remain. Rest the batter 5 minutes so the rice flour hydrates.

instructions.name: Fill and top
instructions.text: Divide batter evenly among the eight lined wells, about 2/3 cup each and no more than three-quarters full. Place two salted-egg wedges on each and scatter with queso fresco.

instructions.name: Bake to a tender set
instructions.text: Bake 22 to 27 minutes, rotating once, until tops are golden, centers spring back and an instant-read thermometer in the center reaches at least 160°F; for a fully set rice-cake crumb, aim for 195 to 200°F without drying the edges.

instructions.name: Finish and serve
instructions.text: Brush the hot cakes lightly with butter and sprinkle with grated coconut and the final 2 tablespoons sugar. Cool in the pan 5 minutes, then lift out by the leaves. Serve warm or at room temperature with the banana-leaf wrappers folded back.

why_it_works: A small amount of glutinous rice flour supplies the gentle chew associated with ground-rice galapong while regular rice flour keeps the cakes tender rather than dense.
Coconut milk, whole milk and butter provide enough fat to keep the rice-flour crumb moist even after the cakes cool.
Pliable banana leaves line each cake without tearing and perfume the batter while reproducing the individual wrapped presentation in the photograph.
swaps: If salted duck eggs are unavailable, use two hard-cooked chicken eggs lightly dusted with salt; the flavor will be milder but the topping remains recognizable.
Pasteurized mild feta can replace queso fresco; rinse and pat it dry first if it is very salty.
For dairy-free cakes, use unsweetened coconut beverage instead of whole milk, vegan butter and a dairy-free salty cheese, checking each package for bake suitability.
storage: Cool completely within 2 hours, then refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 4 days because the cakes contain egg and cheese. Reheat one cake loosely covered at 325°F for 8 to 10 minutes or microwave for 20 to 30 seconds until 165°F. Freeze individually without the coconut finish for up to 2 months.
notes: Use fine rice flour, not gritty cream-of-rice cereal. Glutinous rice flour is naturally gluten-free despite its name, but check labels if cross-contact matters.
Banana leaves can flare over direct flame; use tongs, low heat and only a second or two per section, or soften them safely on a dry skillet.
Cooked salted duck eggs are sold vacuum-packed or in jars at many Asian markets. Confirm they are fully cooked before slicing.
The eight individual cakes match the licensed photograph more closely than one large pan and make serving easier.
Total time includes the five-minute batter rest and five-minute cooling period.

faqs.q: Is bibingka the same as a Western cake?
faqs.a: No. Rice flour and coconut milk give it a tender, lightly chewy crumb rather than the airy crumb of wheat-flour cake. It is often enjoyed warm for breakfast, merienda or holidays.

faqs.q: Can I bake one large bibingka?
faqs.a: Yes. Line a buttered 9-inch round pan with softened banana leaf and bake 32 to 40 minutes, checking for 160°F minimum and a set center. The individual version better matches today's photo and timing.

faqs.q: Why did my banana leaf split?
faqs.a: It was probably too cold or dry. Warm each section until glossy and flexible before folding, and overlap two smaller pieces if a natural tear appears.
